justification: Round-1 capped this at 7.0 for a self-contradictory worked-solution error plus three lower-severity numeric overstatements. I re-derived T(n) = T(n-2) + (n-1) myself from scratch rather than checking the writer's arithmetic: unrolling from T(0)=0 gives T(2k) = k^2 by induction (T(2)=1, T(4)=4, T(6)=9, ...), so at n=8000, k=4000 and T(n)=4000^2=16,000,000 = n^2/4 exactly; the number of additive terms is k = n/2 = 4000, and their average value is T(n)/terms = 16,000,000/4,000 = 4,000 = n/2. That independently confirms the article's revised sentence -- 'roughly n/2 terms, each about n/2 on average ... for a sum of about (n/2)*(n/2) = n^2/4' -- is now self-consistent (the earlier draft's 'n/2 terms averaging just under n' implied a n^2/2 sum that contradicted its own stated 1/4 coefficient; that contradiction is gone). I ran dotnet directly (not just re-reading) on the article's exact duplicates-generator line (const int N = 8000; var rnd = new Random(7); Enumerable.Repeat(0, N).Select(_ => rnd.Next(1, 5)).ToArray()) and got counts 2073 / 1942 / 2032 / 1953 for values 1-4, an exact match to the article's parenthetical -- real, not invented. I hand-traced Partition on a reversed array (pivot = items[lo] = max element, every later element is < pivot, so the scan pointer i walks to hi and the final swap puts the pivot at index hi): the returned pivot index is hi, i.e. the left partition gets all n-1 remaining elements and the right partition gets 0, which is '(n-1):0' as the article now states, not the old, wrong '0:n-1'. I also independently recomputed the average-case gap explanation from the article's own stated double sum (sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (n-k)*2/(k+1), the k=j-i substitution of the printed formula) in a fresh program: exact value at n=8000 is 121,050.73 (article says '≈121,051' -- match), 4.17% from the measured 126,318 (article says 'within about 4%' -- match), while 2*8000*ln(8000) = 143,795.15 (article says '≈143,800' -- match) is 13.84% off (article says 'about 14% off' -- match); this fix correctly reframes the shorthand as a leading-order approximation rather than attributing the whole gap to sampling noise. The duplicates 'a quarter of sorted's naive worst case' fix also checks out: 8,013,935 / 31,996,000 = 25.05%. run-code.mjs passed identically three times in this session (blocks=17 executed=6); since it diffs actual stdout against the article's literal output blocks, its PASS on the four blocks that dropped the CultureInfo/InvariantCulture boilerplate confirms those blocks' N0-formatted (comma thousands separator) output is byte-identical with and without the explicit culture pin on this machine -- the removal changed no output, exactly as the article's explanatory sentence claims. On a fresh full read for anything new: one round-1 finding was NOT addressed. The 'Best case' bullet still links anchor text 'the O(n log n) argument for merge sort' to big-o-notation.md#the-pair-search-does-not-have-to-be-quadratic, and I re-read that target section: it only asserts Array.Sort is O(n log n) by citation and composes it with an O(n) linear scan for a *different* algorithm (a closest-pair search); it never derives or states merge sort's own T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n recurrence. The same article's own text later (its exercise-solution area, 'nothing here proves that merge sort really is Theta(n log n) -- that comes from solving the recursion ... one level up from the rule-of-thumb list above') confirms merge sort's recurrence is not derived anywhere in the current build. This is a real, unfixed moderate issue: the anchor text promises a derivation the target does not contain. I found no other new problems in the full re-read; every quotation, CVE detail, and measured table I re-checked against the article's own code and stated sources held up. Compared with GeeksforGeeks' Quick Sort Algorithm page (still the top-ranking competitor for this query), this article remains substantially deeper and, on the numeric front, now internally consistent everywhere I checked -- but the surviving misleading cross-reference is the kind of thing a strong student or a competent tech editor would still catch, so I am not scoring this at pass threshold yet.
